paragraphs.heading: Choosing and competing
paragraphs.text: Sexual selection is one of the ways evolution works. It has two sides. Members of one sex pick partners from the other sex, which is called intersexual selection, and members of the same sex compete for access to the other sex, which is called intrasexual selection. Both mean that some individuals in a population leave more offspring than others, perhaps because they are better looking, or because they favour better-looking partners.

paragraphs.heading: Why the sexes differ
paragraphs.text: Successful males gain by mating often and by keeping one or more fertile females to themselves. Females get the most out of the energy they spend on reproduction by choosing the best males. This can drive males to great lengths to show they are fit to be chosen, which produces sexual dimorphism: clear differences between the sexes, such as the showy feathers of peafowl and birds-of-paradise or the antlers of deer. In some species these roles are reversed. Sexual selection is common across the animal kingdom and also turns up in plants and fungi.

paragraphs.heading: Darwin and his critics
paragraphs.text: Charles Darwin first proposed the idea in On the Origin of Species in 1859 and developed it in The Descent of Man in 1871. He felt natural selection by itself could not explain some features that do not help an animal survive. He split sexual selection into competition between males and choice by females. Alfred Russel Wallace partly opposed him, mostly after Darwin died. Wallace accepted that sexual selection happened but thought it weak, and he doubted that animals such as beetles could judge beauty.

paragraphs.heading: The runaway loop
paragraphs.text: The statistician and biologist Ronald Fisher built on Darwin's ideas in The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection, a book he published in 1930. He saw that a female's liking for a feature can be passed on genetically together with the genes for the feature itself. Offspring of both sexes inherit both sets of genes. This sets up a loop that feeds itself, called a Fisherian runaway, in which the feature and the taste for it grow together until physical limits stop them.

paragraphs.heading: The long-tailed widowbird
paragraphs.text: The long-tailed widowbird is a classic case. Males grow long tails because females choose them for it, and female taste goes further still: females are drawn to tails longer than any that occur in nature. A female picks the male with the most appealing long tail so that her sons may be attractive to the next generation of females. Those sons can then father many young that carry her genes.

paragraphs.heading: From side issue to major force
paragraphs.text: Biologists did not treat the idea as very important until the 1930s, when they began counting it as a form of natural selection. Even then many leading theorists gave it little attention, and Fisher was the main exception. Only in the 1960s and 1970s, through Robert Trivers and others, did biology come to see it as one of the major drivers of evolution. In the 1990s Marion Petrie showed that peahens chose males with showier plumage. A ten-year study of flour beetles found that sexual selection protected even an inbred population from dying out.
